The target is drawn as an Arduino UNO (the main picture). The manual also shows a Nano, Mega and MKR1000 as other examples, which are not built here.

The 10uF electrolytic capacitor goes between RESET (positive) and GND on the programmer board, because the programmer is an UNO. The manual says to fit it after the ArduinoISP sketch is uploaded. Its legs go straight into the programmer's header sockets (RESET and GND.3).

The three optional status LEDs use the ArduinoISP sketch's default pins: D9 heartbeat, D8 error, D7 programming. The manual does not give resistor values, so 220 ohm is assumed. Each LED has its anode in a column fed by a jumper from the programmer. Its cathode column holds a resistor that goes to the breadboard ground rail (tn). The rail is wired to programmer GND.2.
Breadboard column positions are assumed. The manual's pictures give no hole numbers.

The USB cable is shown on the programmer only, since it needs USB to upload the sketch. The target is powered from the programmer's 5V. The manual says to leave USB and power disconnected while wiring. The computer is not modelled.

The Mega GND used is the one next to AREF (top of the digital header), as drawn in the circuit image.

ISP wiring: Arduino 10 -> reset (pin 1), 11 -> MOSI (pin 17), 12 -> MISO (pin 18), 13 -> SCK (pin 19), per the standard ArduinoISP arrangement. The 10k resistor pulls reset up to 5V.

Power: Arduino 5V and GND go to the top rails, which are bridged to the bottom rails on the right. Power goes to VCC (pin 7), AVCC (pin 20) and GND (pins 8, 22). Pin 20 AVCC and pin 22 GND wiring is inferred from standard practice.
The two blue wires connect the chip's crystal pins (9, 10) to the 16 MHz crystal; each crystal leg also goes to ground via a 22 pF capacitor. Exact positions are assumed.
Chip is drawn as ATmega168 in the image but the text and catalogue use ATmega328P (same pinout).

Powering the Pi itself (USB supply) is mentioned only as 'power up' and is not modelled.
The catalogue lists hc-sr04 with no ports; I used VCC, Trig, Echo and GND, which are the labels on the sensor.
Breadboard banks follow the catalogue: rows f-j are bank 'b' and rows a-e are bank 't'. The sensor sits in columns 1-4 of row j.

The Echo pin goes through a potential divider. 330 ohm (r1) runs from the Echo strip (column 4) to column 8. 470 ohm (r2) runs from column 8 to column 12, and column 12 goes to the ground rail. The divider midpoint (column 8) goes to GPIO17.
The wire positions on the bottom-half ground rail (bn.12, bn.24, bn.28) are estimated from the image.

Pi pins are read from the image. VCC goes to the first 5V pin (physical pin 2, 5V.1), Trig to GPIO4 (pin 7), Echo's divider to GPIO17 (pin 11), and ground to the GND pin at physical pin 39 (GND.8). The text says any numbered GPIO pin works for Trig and Echo.
The 4.000 reading on the sensor in the wiring image is only a display value, so it is not a part.

The breadboard's right-hand rail (used as ground by the black wires, LED cathodes and buzzer) is named 'tn.<n>'. The rail is one strip, so the numbers only approximate the row each part is in. The rail's printed polarity marking is ignored.
Resistor value is not stated. 220 ohm was assumed from the band colours.
Each LED's anode is on the resistor side (column j) and its cathode goes to the ground rail. The 'amber' LED is drawn yellow.

Buzzer positive (marked +) is assumed to be port 1, in row 4 next to the blue wire's strip (4b.j). Its other leg goes to the ground rail.
The Python code and the Traffic HAT / pi-stop alternatives are not part of the build graph.

This is a software-only MakeCode project: no external wiring, breadboard or components are used. The only physical part is the micro:bit, which has its on-board buttons A and B and its 5x5 LED display.

The two images show the loop condition 'while not (button A pressed) and not (button B pressed)'. The Arabic UI labels read: أثناء = while, ليس = not, الزر = button, مضغوط = pressed, و = and, تنفيذ = do.

The code logic is: pause 1000 ms plus a random 0-4000 ms, show an image for 1 s, then wait until A or B is pressed (20 ms pause per loop), then show an arrow for the winner. This logic is not part of the physical build graph.
The micro:bit is not in the catalogue, so I added it as a new part type. I gave the buttons the port kind 'lug' as the closest allowed kind.
The USB cable and computer used to download the .hex file are not described in the manual, so I did not add them.
The optional 'Keep score' challenge uses variables only, so it adds no hardware.

The manual says 'row 1' for both sides of the ravine. I mapped this to column 1, top bank (anode, left of the ravine) and column 1, bottom bank (cathode, right of the ravine), using the catalogue's naming.

Exact holes within a strip are not given. I picked 1t.c for the anode, 1b.f for the cathode, 1b.g for resistor leg 1 (same strip as the cathode), 5b.g for resistor leg 2, 1t.a for the 3V3 wire male end (same strip as the anode) and 5b.h for the GND wire male end (same strip as resistor leg 2).
The manual does not say which 3V3 or GND pin to use. I chose 3V3.1 (pin 1) and GND.1 (pin 6).
The manual gives no resistor value. The resistor type's default is used and no value prop is set.
The LED closeup image shows the flattened edge marking the cathode, so anode and cathode follow the manual's text.
The Raspberry Pi is the power component. Its power supply is not modelled.
Highlighted pins in the image: GND is the left-column pin in the 5th row (physical pin 9 = GND.2); GP17 is the left-column pin in the 6th row (physical pin 11 = GPIO17).
Black wire runs from Pi GND to breadboard hole 15a; purple wire runs from GPIO17 to hole 18a.
The buzzer covers the right part of the top bank, so its legs are assumed to be in column e of rows 15 and 18 (same strips as the wire ends in column a).
Buzzer polarity: port 1 (positive, long leg) is assumed to go to the GPIO17 row (18) and port 2 (negative) to the GND row (15).
No resistor is used, as the manual states. The manual covers the active buzzer, not the passive one.
